stances.reasoning: As Senate President Spilka led passage of the 2022 ROE Act abortion protections bill signed by Gov. Baker, which requires insurers to fully cover abortion and shields providers from out-of-state prosecution. She did not co-sponsor the more expansive Abortion Access Act tracked by Act on Mass (which would go further to remove gestational limits), consistent with her pattern of advancing mainstream but not the most expansive progressive legislation.

No co-sponsorship of the Stop Corporate Offshoring bill or any campaign finance reform bills on the Act on Mass tracker. As Senate President she has not signed the Act on Mass transparency pledge. Her record does not show advocacy for publicly-funded campaigns or strict dark-money limits, but she has supported general legislative transparency measures and has not opposed disclosure requirements.

Spilka co-authored an opinion piece with Senator Jason Lewis advocating for expanded public funding of childcare, stating that like K-12 education, childcare should be a public good. The Senate under her leadership has advanced childcare funding proposals. She stopped short of fully universal publicly-funded childcare but clearly favors major public investment beyond targeted subsidies.

Following George Floyd's murder Spilka created a racial justice advisory group and led passage of police reform legislation addressing police brutality. She received the NAACP's Chaney Goodman Schwerner Advocacy Award in 2020. She championed the Student Opportunity Act providing the largest education funding increase in MA history. Her record shows consistent action on systemic discrimination, though she did not co-sponsor the CARE Act (anti-racism in education).

The Senate under Spilka passed a $3.64 billion environmental bond bill in April 2026. She has not co-sponsored the 100% Renewable Energy by 2045 bill tracked by Act on Mass, and there are reports that she and other officials have grown more cautious on climate commitments amid rising energy costs and ratepayer concerns. Her record shows investment in clean energy but a measured approach rather than rapid decarbonization mandates.

Spilka did not co-sponsor the Safe Communities Act (H.2288/S.1681), which would limit local police cooperation with ICE. In 2018 budget negotiations she and the Speaker could not reach consensus on a measure restricting local police from immigration enforcement, with Spilka unable to deliver the votes. Her public statements criticize the Trump administration's immigration enforcement but she has not championed a formal policy of refusing all deportation cooperation.

Spilka did not co-sponsor the 100% Renewable Energy by 2045 bill. The Senate did pass environmental bond bills under her leadership, but reporting indicates officials including Spilka have become more cautious about fossil fuel phase-out mandates amid rising energy costs. Her record reflects maintenance of current regulations with incremental clean energy investment, not a new-permit ban.

Spilka did not co-sponsor the Medicare for All bill (S.860) tracked by Act on Mass. Her healthcare focus has been on workforce development — e.g. free nursing programs — and expanding access for uninsured populations, consistent with a regulated private-market approach rather than universal public coverage or a public option. No evidence of support for single-payer or comprehensive public option legislation.

No co-sponsorship of the Overdose Prevention Centers bill. Spilka's stated 2025-2026 priorities include primary healthcare delivery and housing affordability but not decriminalization of public sleeping or major enforcement-to-services redirects. Her approach appears to be maintaining existing shelter infrastructure while investing incrementally rather than decriminalizing or defunding enforcement.

Senate under Spilka unveiled a housing plan in 2024 that explicitly excluded a real estate transfer tax, a provision housing advocates wanted for affordable unit funding. She has supported housing production broadly but her chamber took a more market-oriented approach than housing advocates preferred. No co-sponsorship of the Lift the Ban on Local Tenant Protections bill. Reflects targeted subsidies and permitting reform over rent control or large public housing investments.

Spilka did not co-sponsor the Safe Communities Act. In 2018, she was unable to get the Senate to restrict local police from immigration enforcement during budget negotiations. She has verbally opposed the Trump administration's immigration actions but has not championed expansive legal immigration pathways or broad services for undocumented immigrants beyond the driver's license law that passed in 2022.

Spilka did not co-sponsor the Prison Moratorium, Age of Criminal Majority to 21, or Life Without Parole reform bills tracked by Act on Mass, though she did mention expanding juvenile court jurisdiction to include 18-year-olds as a 2025 priority. She led a 2013 effort raising the juvenile age from 17 to 18. Her record reflects incremental reforms rather than transformational decarceration.

Did not co-sponsor the Safe Communities Act (S.1681), which would limit police cooperation with ICE. As Senate President she controls the calendar and has kept the bill from coming to a floor vote despite advocacy. Her stated position — criticizing federal immigration enforcement while not legislating sanctuary protections — is consistent with following federal law without proactive city/state enforcement cooperation.

Did not co-sponsor the Medicare for All bill. No evidence of support for expanding Medicare eligibility age or major Medicaid expansion beyond current parameters. Her healthcare agenda focuses on workforce and access rather than structural expansion of public programs. Consistent with improving current programs while controlling costs.

Spilka has not co-sponsored or publicly championed independent redistricting commission legislation. As Senate President she controls the chamber where such bills would need to pass, and MA remains under legislative control of redistricting. She drew criticism for lack of transparency in the 2021 redistricting process. Consistent with state legislature retaining redistricting power with court oversight but without independent citizen commission.

No evidence of extremes in either direction on religious freedom. Spilka has supported LGBTQ protections and described herself as an early supporter of same-sex marriage, but there is no record of legislation strictly separating religion from public institutions or, conversely, allowing broad faith-based exemptions. Her record reflects the balanced mainstream Democratic approach.

Spilka voted in 2004 when she was a state representative to make Massachusetts the first state to legalize same-sex marriage. She describes herself as an 'early and ardent supporter of equal marriage and transgender protections.' This is a defining vote and consistent career-long position.

Spilka championed MassReconnect (free community college for residents 25+) in 2023 and expanded it to all residents in 2024, investing heavily in public higher education. Her education agenda is centered on public school funding — the Student Opportunity Act provided the largest K-12 funding increase in state history. No evidence of support for voucher programs; her record consistently prioritizes public education investment.

Spilka co-authored a 2023 op-ed with House Speaker Mariano supporting the 'Commonwealth's largest tax relief package in a generation,' which included across-the-board cuts. She did not co-sponsor the Stop Corporate Offshoring bill (progressive revenue measure). Her record shows some targeted tax cuts alongside modest investments, consistent with closing loopholes and maintaining current rates rather than significantly raising or cutting taxes.

Spilka describes herself as an 'early and ardent supporter of transgender protections.' Massachusetts passed the 2016 gender identity anti-discrimination law protecting trans people in public accommodations under her Senate leadership. No evidence she has supported restricting transgender athletes. Her consistent pro-trans-rights record places her in support of allowing trans athletes to compete on teams matching gender identity.

The Massachusetts Senate under Spilka's leadership passed permanent mail-in voting and expanded early voting in 2021-2022. She has not co-sponsored the Voting Rights Restoration bill (restoring voting rights for incarcerated people, tracked by Act on Mass). Her record supports expanding early and mail-in voting access without requiring automatic registration or restoring incarcerated voting rights.
